note: The ENFORCEMENT GAP registry. Vocabulary fixed by Justin 2026-08-08: a STANDARD is a rule we enforce; a SURFACE is a place enforcement can act; a MOMENT is when a surface acts; an ENFORCEMENT FINGERPRINT is a standard's recorded mapping of surfaces to moments plus what its violations look like; an ENFORCEMENT GAP is a recorded FAILURE-SHAPE — the way a violation slipped past a fingerprint. A gap is evidence about fingerprints, not about one standard: it is swept against EVERY fingerprinted standard so one failure upgrades every standard sharing the hole-shape. A sweep records the population it ran against, so adding a fingerprint STALES every sweep and forces the new standard to be checked against every known shape. See scripts/lint-enforcement-gap-records.mjs. Both terms are namespaced deliberately (external review pass 2, finding 6): bare `gap` already names *Architectural Agency in the Gap* in this constitution and bare `fingerprint` already denotes a routing identity in the system, so the unqualified words carry two meanings each.

gaps.shapeDescription: The moment is WATCHED — a live surface sits there and its stated population plausibly reaches the violation — and the violation passes anyway, and the surface records no per-decision verdict, so nobody can distinguish 'the rule fired and was overridden' from 'it never fired' from 'it fired and judged wrongly'. **The shape is the unauditability, not a claim about coverage.** (Corrected 2026-08-09: this field previously read "The moment IS covered" while the evidence field beneath it said coverage is unknown — the record asserting and withdrawing the same claim in adjacent fields, which review pass 5 caught and which is the internal contradiction this registry exists to make impossible.) A fingerprint has this shape when it names a surface that leaves no trace of what it decided.

evaded.standard: Self-Unblock Before Escalating (which carried NO enforcement fingerprint — see note)
evaded.how: **CORRECTED (review pass 4): this record originally said the failure evaded that article's FINGERPRINT. It had none — none existed anywhere at the time — so the record asserted a mechanism that did not exist, which is manufactured enforcement inside the registry built to catch it.** What actually happened, stated without the invented mechanism: five tone-gate rules classified `blocking` sit at the outbound moment — B15_CONTEXT_DEATH_STOP, B16_UNVERIFIED_WALL, B17_FALSE_BLOCKER, B18_AUTONOMY_STOP, B19_PARKED_ON_USER — the gate was demonstrably live (it held one of my own messages the same day), and the 2026-08-07 violation went through. **Whether any of those rules should have fired is UNKNOWN and unknowable from the record**, because nothing on disk captures which rules were evaluated or what each returned; the advisory log captures only the deterministic preflight layer (`advisories: []`, `action: "clean"`). The earlier phrasing said their populations "plausibly cover" the manifestation and then treated that as coverage. It is not: *Self-Unblock* withdrew the coverage assertion the same day on the evidence that its own motivating violation passed the live gate. **The shape this gap records is therefore the absence of a VERDICT RECORD, not a claim about what the rules cover.**
evaded.hadNoFingerprintNote: **hadNoFingerprint: true.** Set 2026-08-09 when a new arm found that EVERY gap record here named a standard with no enforcement fingerprint — review pass 4 caught one instance, the mechanism then found all five. No standard carried a fingerprint until this window created the field, so nothing recorded before it can honestly have EVADED one. What these records actually document is a failure that got past whatever was in place, which is a weaker and true claim.

correctionLog.what: GAP-alive-but-inert vs Iterative Audit to Convergence: matched -> unmatched
correctionLog.why: The MATCH was asserted from the shape of the citation without checking whether a negative control existed. It did. The sweep check accepted the verdict because a verdict requires a REASON and not EVIDENCE — a hole in this registry's own machinery, found by making the exact error the registry exists to catch, inside the registry, one hour after building it. Reasons are cheap; the pattern that produced the true finding four hours earlier was INJECTION-TESTING, and I skipped it here because the shape felt familiar. A precise diagnosis suppresses the second opinion, which is why it raises the bar for checking rather than lowering it.

gaps.shapeDescription: A dispatch withholds its ANSWER — satisfying the protocol on its face — while supplying, as established observation, the one PREMISE the answer turns on. The reviewer then tests everything except the load-bearing claim, because it arrived as context rather than as a question. The output looks like independent judgement and is not. A guard has this shape when it checks that a protocol is PRESENT rather than that the premises were withheld — presence of the ritual standing in for the property.

evaded.standard: A Dispatch Supplies the Question and Withholds the Answer
evaded.how: The sovereignty referral was convened precisely because its author benefits from the answer, and it carried the protocol correctly: the question was posed as an explicit a/b/c and the preferred answer was named as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion — which reads as bias-avoidance. But the dispatch also stated that the symptom "appears to be evaluated on every outbound message already ... a check on real behaviour rather than on the existence of anything." That is the single fact that would make (a) correct, it was supplied as observation, and it is FALSE — the judgement is gated behind a seventeen-phrase substring pre-filter. A reviewer who accepted the framing instead of reading the code returns (a) and makes exactly the manufactured citation the referral existed to prevent. **The referral caught it and said so, about its own convener.** scripts/lint-dispatch-withholds-answer.mjs cannot see it: it verifies the protocol's presence in templated dispatches, and this dispatch HAD the protocol.

gaps.residual: Nothing detects a planted premise. The lint checks protocol presence; only a reviewer reading the underlying code instead of the dispatch's framing catches it — which is what happened here, and is not a guarantee.

gaps.shapeDescription: A correction narrows the defect and then RESTATES the over-claim it was correcting, inside the sentence announcing the fix. The gap shrinks — often by a large factor — while the CLAIM stays at 100%, so the artifact that certifies the defect is gone is itself the new instance of it. It survives review because a reader checks whether the fix happened, not whether the fix's own description is now true. A guard or a record has this shape when its correction note asserts full coverage rather than the coverage actually attained.

evaded.standard: Verify the State, Not Its Symbol
evaded.how: Three instances in one day, in the same file, each while fixing the previous one, and NONE caught by me. (i) The deferral guard matched two numeric id forms in prose while its prose claimed to police tracked deferrals — 47% of the real population; caught by external review pass 1. (ii) The fix took the MARKER but kept the commit-time step's character class, which a SPACE terminates, so 25 live markers with a space, comma or parenthesis stayed invisible — 89% coverage, and the sentence announcing the correction said it saw the subject; caught by an independent lane that re-derived the count and refused to accept mine. (iii) The gap registry's own certification clause listed one limitation when four applied; caught by external review pass 2. The through-line is not carelessness about the mechanism — each mechanism genuinely improved — it is that the DESCRIPTION is written in the moment of relief at having fixed the thing, and nobody re-measures a sentence.

gaps.shapeDescription: A guard's population is keyed on a HUMAN-EDITABLE NAME — an article heading, a marker id, a slug — and the container holding it keeps one entry per key. Two distinct things given the same name therefore COLLAPSE into one slot, and the collapse buys both directions at once: the later entry is admitted to the enforced population without ever being examined, and the earlier one silently stops being watched, because the survivor occupies its slot. The guard reports clean throughout, and the count it publishes is the count of NAMES rather than of THINGS — so the number that would expose the collapse is typically already computed and already on screen, compared to nothing. A fingerprint has this shape when any surface it cites builds a Set or Map keyed on a name a human can choose freely, and does not refuse a repeat.

evaded.standard: One Failure Teaches Every Guard — Record the Shape, Sweep It Everywhere
evaded.how: Found by an INDEPENDENT reviewer (the laptop lane) by execution, not by reading, and reproduced end-to-end here before any repair. A seventh standard was appended to the registry under a heading IDENTICAL to one of the six already fingerprinted, carrying its own fingerprint line. `scripts/lint-enforcement-fingerprint.mjs` printed clean at seven fingerprinted, with no objection to the repeated name. `scripts/lint-enforcement-gap-records.mjs` objected only SIDEWAYS — that a content digest had changed — and its remedy line said to re-sweep and paste the new digest. **Complying with the guard's own printed instruction was the step that completed the exploit:** both guards then reported clean, five gaps swept, against a live population of seven, while the five sweeps between them reached a verdict on six. All four existing arms miss it for a reason worth recording, because 'we have four checks' was exactly the feeling of coverage: the staleness arm asks whether a live NAME is absent from the swept set and both entries share the name; the partition arm compares the sweep against its own recorded population, which is a set of names, so it partitions perfectly; the content-address arm is the one that should catch it and is precisely the one the collision defeats, since a Map holds one digest per name; and the floor arm has no opinion about articles. The second direction was then demonstrated too: with the collision in place, the ORIGINAL article's fingerprint was rewritten to read `moments: none; surfaces: none whatsoever` and NOTHING went stale. **Honest bound on the evasion:** the build never actually went green — `scripts/lint-no-duplicate-definitions.mjs` refuses a repeated article heading and fails first, which was verified against the attacked tree rather than assumed. But that coverage was BORROWED: it parses the registry separately and, unlike the two fingerprint guards, unwraps blockquotes before matching, so the three populations agreed by coincidence and nothing recorded or re-checked the coupling.

sweep.method: For each fingerprinted standard, read every surface it cites and ask: does that surface build its population in a container keyed on a name a human chooses freely (heading, marker id, slug), and does it refuse a repeat? Where the answer was reachable by execution the verdict was EARNED by execution rather than by reading the code, because this window has repeatedly shown a code-read agreeing with a claim the run then falsifies.

matched.standard: One Failure Teaches Every Guard — Record the Shape, Sweep It Everywhere
matched.why: This is where the shape was found, and the repair for it took THREE attempts, each one an instance of the shape it was fixing. (1) A duplicate-name check covering only the half of the collision space where the duplicate ALSO carries a fingerprint — review pass 10 walked the other half through. (2) That check plus a partition assertion certified as the real general repair — review pass 11 proved the partition UNREACHABLE on every input (9,330 modelled populations, zero reaching it), because the name check preempted it. (3) CONSOLIDATION: the partition alone refuses both halves, so the name check contributed no coverage and only preempted the partition into silence. Two checks were never two things. What stands in the frozen tree is ONE refusal, whose condition is the partition arithmetic and whose message names the duplicate headings. It is NOT a broader net than name-uniqueness — it catches exactly what a duplicate-name rule catches, and the arithmetic form buys resilience to a refactor and nothing else.
matched.evidence: Re-reached 2026-08-09 after review pass 12 found this field still describing a "name arm" that the freeze commit had DELETED, and citing as proof a source-mutation my own commit body had already disowned. The current evidence, all fired by INPUTS rather than by editing the guard: attack A (duplicate heading, both fingerprinted) refused — "89 article(s), but 6 fingerprinted + 82 without a fingerprint = 88"; attack B (duplicate heading, the new article carrying no fingerprint) refused identically; a heading indented one to three spaces refused by the dialect check, with fenced and HTML-commented examples correctly NOT refused; the untouched registry clean at 88 / 6 / 82. NEGATIVE CONTROL BY REMOVAL, which is the first honest one this arm has had: delete the surviving refusal and BOTH attacks report clean. KNOWN NOT COVERED, stated rather than left to be found: a duplicate heading where NEITHER article carries a fingerprint is not caught by this refusal — it is caught by the shrink-only baseline arm and by the sibling duplicate-definitions lint, so net coverage is unchanged, but the credit belongs to the chain and not to this guard.

matched.why: The shape is PRESENT and this is the loop paying for itself — one failure in one standard's machinery taught me about a different standard's guard. `scripts/lint-deferral-referent-resolves.mjs` builds `declared` as a Map from marker id to a Set of spec paths, and `resolved` as a Set of ids, so two genuinely DIFFERENT promises that are given the same tracked id collapse into one entry: resolving either one clears both. Its clean line then reports a count of IDS, not of promises, which is the same publish-the-key-count defect. Recorded as a match rather than patched, because two markers sharing an id are OFTEN deliberately the same promise cited twice, and that is a design question about promise identity rather than an obvious bug — inventing a guard for it tonight would be the manufactured enforcement this registry refuses.
matched.evidence: ran it: two distinct promises in docs/specs/alpha.md and docs/specs/beta.md both marked ZZZ-90001, with only the first implemented in src/, produced `clean — 1 tracked deferral id(s), 1 resolve, 0 orphaned` while the backup promise was never implemented anywhere

unmatched.why: Immune deliberately rather than by luck, which is the distinction this sweep exists to draw. Its cited surface `scripts/write-audit-convergence.mjs` builds a registry article index and REFUSES the collision up front: a repeated article title returns `duplicate standards article title ... is ambiguous`, and a repeated Article ID returns a duplicate-owner error, both before the index is built. The audit slug itself cannot collapse either — the slug must equal the file basename, so the filesystem holds one record per slug and a second audit under one slug is a visible overwrite rather than a silent merge.

gaps.residual: Two things this record does NOT close. First, the matched instance on *Deferral = Deletion* is recorded and unfixed by choice — two markers sharing an id may be one promise cited twice, so the repair needs a decision about promise identity rather than a reflex. Second, and larger: this sweep asked the question of the SIX fingerprinted standards, and name-keyed populations are everywhere in this repository — the eighty-two grandfathered articles were not examined, and no mechanism finds a name-keyed container that lacks a uniqueness refusal. The shape is now recorded and will be asked of every future fingerprint by the staleness arm; it is not retroactively swept across the codebase, and stating that is cheaper than discovering it later.

gaps.shapeDescription: A guard STATES, in its own routine output, that it is not doing the thing it exists to do — and the statement is printed so often, on so many successful runs, that a reader stops seeing it. This is NOT alive-but-inert: there the signal is absent, so nobody could have known. Here the signal is present, correct, honest, emitted every single time, and read as part of the normal all-clear. The failure is not detectability but ATTENTION — the announcement becomes wallpaper, and its position beside a success line teaches the reader that it IS a success line. A fingerprint has this shape when any surface it cites emits, on its ROUTINE PASS path, a sentence conceding reduced coverage, a skipped step, an inactive arm, or an outstanding debt.

evaded.how: CORRECTED by review pass 15, which was right and which I had to check rather than accept. This record originally asserted `hadNoFingerprint: false` — a claim that a real fingerprint was got past — and it is only the second of 7 records to claim that (review pass 16 caught "eight" here — there are 7; the figure was carried out of a probe's own output line into prose, which is a count-about-itself error inside the record family whose guard exists for exactly that). It is not true. The specimen is `scripts/pre-push-smoke.mjs` at PUSH-TIME; the named fingerprint declares `moments: commit-time, ci-time` and cites `scripts/write-audit-convergence.mjs` plus the commit gate and CI. Neither the moment nor the surface matches. Worse, that fingerprint's own coverage argument ALREADY says "Running a single pass and never opening an audit record at all is NOT covered by anything" — so the failure did not evade a guard, it landed in a hole the article had already declared honestly. Recording it as an evasion took credit, for the registry, that the registry had explicitly disclaimed. What actually happened: a skipped smoke run silently converted an audit-shaped obligation (run the whole surface) into a single-pass check, at a moment nothing watches. The guard cannot catch this class of error either — `lint-enforcement-gap-records.mjs` validates that `evaded.standard` names a fingerprinted article but never compares `atMoment` against that fingerprint's DECLARED moments, so this passed clean. That gap in the gap-guard is now itself named in the residual.
evaded.hadNoFingerprintNote: CORRECTED AGAIN by review pass 16, which is right on both halves and which I verified before accepting. (i) The flag is MECHANICALLY INERT here: the guard only consults it when `evaded.standard` fails to resolve, and "Iterative Audit to Convergence" does resolve, so all four states of this field pass identically. (ii) It is FALSE under the schema's own definition, which is "the named standard carries no enforcement fingerprint" — that article IS fingerprinted, as the note beside it already conceded. So withdrawing a manufactured-enforcement claim was recorded as a schema claim that is false under the schema, with zero effect. It is left TRUE deliberately rather than flipped back, because `false` asserts the stronger thing (a real fingerprint was got past) and that is the claim pass 15 refuted; but the honest statement is neither value — the schema has no way to express "the named standard is fingerprinted, and its fingerprint does not reach this moment or surface". That missing expressiveness, and the missing `atMoment`-vs-declared-moments check that would catch it, are named in the residual rather than papered over with whichever boolean reads better.

sweep.method: For each fingerprinted standard, run its cited surfaces and read their ROUTINE PASS output, not their failure output. Ask: does the successful run emit a sentence conceding reduced coverage, a skipped arm, or standing debt — something a reader would habituate to because it appears beside an all-clear? Verdicts were taken from executed output rather than from reading the source, because the whole shape is about what a surface SAYS on a normal day.

It announces 201 unresolved promises and prefixes that announcement with the word CLEAN. The concession is not hidden — it is the majority of the sentence — and it is emitted on every successful run of the whole lint chain, which is how a reader learns to read `201 orphaned` as part of an all-clear rather than as the standing debt it is. This is the same habituation that cost me the pre-push line, on a surface inside the fingerprinted population.

gaps.residual: Nothing detects this shape, and it is not obvious that anything mechanically can: the offending text is HONEST, and a guard flagging every candid concession would flag most of the good ones. The three matched instances are recorded as findings rather than repaired, because the repair is a judgement about which concessions belong on a pass path at all. FOUR things this record got wrong and had corrected, kept because the pattern is the finding: (1) it claimed an evaded fingerprint where the fingerprint declares neither the moment nor the surface, and had already disclaimed that coverage in writing; (2) its one substantive unmatch verdict was falsified by the very guard it exonerated, once a legal unswept gap existed to produce the line; (3) `lint-enforcement-gap-records.mjs` validates that `evaded.standard` names a fingerprinted article but NEVER compares `evaded.atMoment` against that article's declared moments, which is how (1) passed clean — an unenforced sub-obligation of the gap guard itself, named here rather than left; (4) the originating specimen sits OUTSIDE the fingerprinted population entirely, so the sweep found relatives of a defect it could never have found itself. The habituation cost was not theoretical: it is why a red branch survived fourteen adversarial reviews, thirteen of which never ran the suite.
